name: MM.104

origin.place: East Malling Research Station and John Innes Institute, Merton
origin.note: Bred in the joint East Malling / John Innes woolly aphid programme; introduced 1952.

soil_notes: Only for freely drained soils; very prone to collar rot where water lies.
best_for: large free-standing trees on well-drained soils in mild climates
avoid_when: heavy or poorly drained soils; cold-winter regions; small gardens
variety_fit: Tends to give a broad, spreading tree.
notes: A vigorous woolly-aphid-resistant stock giving trees close to seedling size, well anchored and propagating freely in the stoolbed. Its very high susceptibility to collar rot led to it being largely replaced by MM.111. It survives mainly in older plantings and in drier regions such as Western Australia; hardiness and fire blight data are thin.

name: MM.109

origin.place: East Malling Research Station and John Innes Institute, Merton
origin.note: Sister line of MM.104 from the joint East Malling / John Innes programme; introduced 1952.

soil_notes: Suited to lighter, low-to-medium fertility soils and dryland sites; avoid poorly drained ground because of collar rot.
best_for: large trees on poor, sandy or replant soils in warm climates; spur-type varieties
avoid_when: wet or heavy soils; cold-winter regions; small gardens
variety_fit: Recommended in South Africa for spur types and weak growers on poor soils.
notes: A very vigorous woolly-aphid-resistant stock, about seedling size, that has been surprisingly precocious and heavy cropping for its vigour in Australian and South African trials. It is used mainly in warm, dry regions on poor or replant soils. It is susceptible to collar rot, moderately resistant to fire blight, and its cold hardiness is not well documented.

name: M.25

origin.note: Bred at East Malling (hence the M rather than MM prefix) and introduced in 1952; unlike the MM stocks it was not selected for woolly aphid resistance.

support: Strong stake and guard for the first 2-3 years; then free-standing
soil_notes: Copes with grass competition and lower fertility; best on deep, reasonably drained soil; growth suffers on waterlogged or very dry sites.
best_for: traditional standard orchards, cider orchards, grazed or grassed orchards, heritage replanting
avoid_when: gardens or any site without room for a 6-7 m tree; waterlogged ground
variety_fit: Gives the largest crops with cider and traditional standard varieties; useful for spur types and weak growers on replant ground.
notes: The most vigorous Malling stock, producing full-size standard trees for traditional and cider orchards, with good anchorage and cropping that starts earlier than seedling stocks. It has some resistance to collar rot but, despite its Northern Spy parent, is susceptible to woolly aphid. Hardiness and fire blight data are limited.

name: M.2

origin.parentage: old Doucin stock of French origin
origin.note: Sorted and numbered at East Malling from 1912; long the standard UK stock for bush trees before MM.106, and a parent of MM.104, MM.109, M.25 and Merton 793.

support: Stake in early years; free-standing after, though trees may lean on heavy clay
soil_notes: Does best in moisture-retentive loam; tends to lean in heavy clay.
best_for: large bush and half-standard trees; restoring historic plantings
avoid_when: small gardens; dry, light soils; where woolly aphid is a problem
variety_fit: In UK work, Cox on M.2 was singled out as prone to collar rot even though M.2 itself rated resistant.
notes: An old, vigorous Doucin-type stock that was the mainstay for UK bush trees until MM.106 and MM.111 replaced it. It is free-standing, moderately slow to crop, and fairly resistant to collar rot in UK trials, but susceptible to woolly aphid. Its main modern importance is as a parent of several later stocks.

name: M.4

origin.parentage: old Doucin stock of unknown origin (name suggests Holstein, northern Germany)
origin.note: Sorted and numbered at East Malling from 1912; widely used in the Netherlands and Germany in the mid-20th century.

support: Stake or support recommended; trees tend to lean
soil_notes: Described as widely adapted; anchorage is the main limitation.
best_for: historic or collection plantings of semi-vigorous bush trees
avoid_when: exposed, windy sites without support; mown ground where suckers are a nuisance
notes: A semi-vigorous Doucin stock, fairly precocious and productive, that was popular in Dutch and German orchards before dwarfing stocks took over. Its well-known fault is a one-sided root system that lets trees lean, and it suckers moderately to heavily. Collar rot resistance and fire blight tolerance are rated good; it is susceptible to woolly aphid. US sources give larger sizes (75-85% of seedling) than European ones.

name: M.1

origin.parentage: old English paradise stock, recorded in England around 1860
origin.note: First of the paradise types sorted and numbered at East Malling from 1912; a parent of MM.106.

avoid_when: any modern planting: superseded by MM.106 and MM.111
notes: A vigorous old English paradise stock, classed as vigorous at East Malling and semi-dwarf to semi-standard in later US summaries, with moderate winter hardiness. Like the other early Malling types it is susceptible to woolly aphid. It is now essentially obsolete and remembered mainly as a parent of MM.106; most performance traits are poorly documented.
